argument_summary: The supportable certification position is narrow: admissible evidence supports launch readiness in aggregate, but not an unqualified claim of full policy satisfaction on the telehealth discharge planning slice. The defensible reading is that certification can be treated as caveated only if the audit packet records the current subgroup limitation as an unresolved governance condition rather than implying that prior approval, informal monitoring, or aggregate performance closes that gap. On that basis, the decision should not escalate as a broader launch-readiness failure, but it also should not be described as clean compliance.
claims_about_business_cost: No business-cost argument is relied on. The position rests on risk-weighted interpretation of the existing admissible record, not on urgency or rollout pressure.
claims_about_policy: The policy does not permit prior approval or an informal monitoring note to substitute for current-release documentation or approved mitigation. The admissible record does support a narrower conclusion: aggregate readiness and rehearsal results justify certification in general, while the telehealth regression must remain explicitly identified as a current documentation/governance gap. That supports caveated treatment, not a finding that the record already demonstrates full compliance.
concessions: The current record does not show that the release documentation actually includes the required disclosure for the telehealth discharge planning weakness.
The current record does not show an approved mitigation or reviewed risk acceptance covering that specific subgroup regression.
Aggregate readiness and no severity-one rehearsal incidents do not, by themselves, satisfy the disclosure-or-mitigation requirement for the named use-case weakness.
